posts.c: Punk rock icon Henry Rollins (@fanatichenry) moved to Nashville, the country music capital of the world, five years ago. He had built up a collection of punk posters, photographs and ephemera. Recently he produced a free show of his collection. This exhibition title? Cool Evidence. The 65-year old Rollins wanted to do a punk museum in Nashville. But after crunching the numbers he decided on a series of traveling pop-ups around the world. Music and Culture reporter Justin Barney (@justinbarney) attended the show. There were lines to get in that snaked around the gallery. The walls were chock full of colorful band posters. And they each had a written description from Rollins himself. And in the middle of the gallery, the biggest crowd was around Rollins himself, who held court all night, explaining his ethos for doing this. “Now that I’m old, my job is to find ways to release joy. I owe history to get this stuff out in front of people.” And in 2028, he hopes to take the exhibition on tou
posts.hd: Henry Rollins shows his punk collection in Nashville

posts.c: Facing backlash over what some fans called “a cheap attempt at shock value,” HBO period drama The Gilded Age was reportedly under fire Monday for a scene depicting an ugly hat. “I can’t believe my eyes—where the hell has this show gone?” said frustrated viewer Rachel King, whose post on the r/television subreddit elicited thousands of responses from like-minded fans who felt sick to their stomachs after catching a glimpse of the lackluster costume accessory. “There’s no excuse for that kind of tasteless headwear. How could the producers let this happen? I understand that ugly hats were a real thing that existed at the time, but this was a gratuitous display of bad fashion that added nothing to the narrative. I am so done.” At press time, Gilded Age fans confirmed they had decided to give the series one more chance after seeing a gorgeous hat.
posts.hd: Satirical headline about Gilded Age ugly hat

posts.c: Over the past year, seven people were killed in crashes while biking, walking, and rolling on Vermont roadways: Mauricio Martinez, Janet Spencer, Kylee Bean, Owen Rich, Devin Pierro, Shiloh Skalka, and Todd Ward. On this World Day of Remembrance, we honor them, as well as the 139 more injured, and the impact left on their families, friends, and communities. It doesn’t have to be this way. What can you do? Know where to go in a time of crisis. Connect with advocates in your community, and stay connected with your walking/biking/rolling community - especially in the coming winter months. Find all of these resources, and our full report on the World Day of Remembrance at the link in our bio. #WDoR2026 #SafetyNotSpeed

posts.c: From the traditional music of Colombia's Pacific coast to Tego Calderón and Nigerian Afrobeats star Burna Boy, Colombian artist @jossmansaac takes us on a musical journey across the African diaspora. Recorded live in Bogotá during @bogotamusicmarket 2026, this episode of El Sonido: Cancioneros explores the connections between Timbiquí, the Caribbean, and Nigeria through the music that shaped Jossman's identity as a singer, songwriter, and producer. Known as AFROKING, Jossman has spent years building bridges between contemporary Afrobeats and the musical traditions of Colombia's Pacific coast. His 2025 album AFROKING brings those worlds together through collaborations with artists including Nidia Góngora and Grupo Canalón de Timbiquí. 📺 Watch the full video episode on the KEXP Podcasts YouTube channel or listen wherever you get your podcasts. Support El Sonido at kexp.org/el-sonido.

posts.c: 🛘 DJ Shadow | Friday, March 19 🎫 On sale Friday at 10 📢 HG presale Wednesday at 12 _ DJ Shadow (Josh Davis) is a pioneering producer and DJ known for his groundbreaking use of sampling, deep crate-digging, and genre-defying approach to hip-hop, electronic, and experimental music. His 1996 debut, Endtroducing..., was the first album composed entirely of samples, earning a Guinness World Record and influencing generations of artists. Featuring classics like Midnight in a Perfect World and Building Steam with a Grain of Salt, it remains one of the most celebrated instrumental hip-hop records of all time. Following Endtroducing..., Shadow evolved his sound with The Private Press (2002), featuring the cult hit Six Days. He expanded further with The Outsider (2006), incorporating Bay Area hyphy influences and collaborating with E-40, Q-Tip, and David Banner. posts.c: Vermonters might be surprised by just how many of their neighbors have been dancing their way to connection and joy. From Hardwick to Rutland to Burlington, teachers and organizers say their weekly or monthly dances sometimes attract upwards of 100 attendees, typically a mix of dedicated dancers and newbies. Whatever the dance style, these “dance socials” or “open dances” have a few things in common. Everyone is welcome, regardless of experience level; the point is to have fun, not to be perfect; and participants are encouraged to mingle and dance with strangers rather than stick with friends or romantic partners. In many cases, brief lessons precede the gatherings, giving everybody a few steps on which to build. We talked to some organizers and attendees of line dancing, honky-tonk, and Latin and African partner-dance socials — just some of the styles offered around Vermont. Contra dances also frequently draw huge crowds, and there are robust West Coast Swing and Lindy Hop communities

posts.c: My neighbor practically gave me this board so I'm doing my best to use it. It comes from an era where everything was made with big transformer preamps, and so models like this took on the colloquial name of "japa-neve", referencing the Rupert Neve design preamps (1073 and the like). Seeing as I've been on the dl looking for a 1073 style preamp, it could be a match made in heaven or it could be a total bust! I'm not about to debate that preamps are worthwhile to invest in. They almost certainly are not for the large majority of songwriters or home producers as most listeners, including audiophiles, probably couldn't tell the difference between a track that was produced with a thousand dollar preamp or your average focusrite 2i2. That said, I am (unfortunately) now able to hear the difference and so I want to have the option to use them if I can.

posts.c: In Vermont, the sugarhouse is a kind of sacred place: a steamy little cabin at the edge of the woods where sap becomes syrup and neighbors gather while the fire burns. It is fitting, then, that the state’s most talked-about new hotel takes its name and its spirit from them. @sugarhousehotelvt has opened in Winooski, a historic mill city just across the river from Burlington, and it is the first hotel the city has ever had. It is also something Marriott has never done anywhere in the world: a hotel designed from the start to run entirely on electricity, produce as much energy as it uses over the course of a year and earn LEED Platinum certification. And yet the first thing you notice isn’t the technology. It’s the timber, the glass and the sense that every corner was made by someone who lives nearby. → Read the full story on 5 Reasons to Visit. #travel #destination #vermont #winooski #newengland

posts.c: 💕 Did you know that WHERE you pet your dog matters? Our furry friends have their own preferences when it comes to physical touch! Some enjoy gentle chest rubs, chin scratches, and soft pets around the base of the neck. 🐾 Usually loved: Gentle chest rubs, chin scratches, and soft strokes along the back. ⚠️ Be careful with: Reaching over the head, touching the paws, hugging tightly, or pulling the tail. These actions can make some dogs feel uncomfortable or trapped. 💙 Every dog is different, so watch their body language and let them choose when they want affection. 👇 Question: Where does your dog love being petted the most?

posts.c: Every dad has given this exact look at least once 😂 Music production has become much more accessible in recent years, with software called a DAW (Digital Audio Workstation) allowing anyone with a laptop to create, record, and mix their own beats and tracks from home. What once required an expensive professional studio can now be done on a bedroom desk, which is why so many young people have picked it up as a hobby or even a career path. For parents, it can be hard to tell whether all those hours staring at a screen and tweaking sounds is serious creative work or just a very convincing way to avoid the dishes. (🎥/ @v.v.j._trey )

posts.c: The flies didn’t stand a chance 😂 Salt guns are handheld devices designed to shoot a small burst of regular table salt at insects, killing or stunning them on contact. They are popular because the salt disperses quickly and leaves no toxic residue, making them safer to use around food than chemical sprays. The range and spread of the salt means they work best at close distances, and while they are effective against flies and similar insects, they do leave a light dusting of salt on whatever surface is nearby, which can be a small downside at the dinner table. (🎥/ @lindybowbindy )

posts.c: Presented by National Geographic Society in partnership with @Rolex. Pygmy blue whales compete with fin whales for the title of the second-largest animal in the world. They typically roam the world’s oceans, but one group off the coast of New Zealand seems to have settled in the South Taranaki Bight. To better understand the behavior of these marine giants, researchers are studying some of the ocean’s smallest creatures—swarms of krill thriving in the whales’ new home. They hope that by understanding the relationship between the two, they can better understand the effects that warming waters will have on them. Learn more about this mysterious group of whales at the link in bio. Rolex and the National Geographic Society are partnering on select science-based expeditions to explore, study, and document change in the planet’s unique regions. #PerpetualPlanet. Videos by National Geographic Society/Impact Story Lab; Photographs by @ralphpace

posts.c: “I don’t think about the listener. I just make it because I want to make it.” As part of EMERGENT with Levi’s®, Yuki Chiba (@yukichiba_) talks about making music without overthinking it, from improvising in the studio to songwriting as a way of documenting life as it happens. Set reminder for the premiere via the link in bio.

9 years ago, we made a song called Santorini. At the time, it became our most successful release, finding its way around the world and reaching over 2 million streams. We never could have imagined that almost a decade later we’d find ourselves standing in the very place that inspired its name. It felt surreal making music together in the studio to watching the sun set over the Aegean Sea, surrounded by blue domes, and walking through the whitewashed streets. A pretty special full circle moment. Forever grateful for the music, the memories, and the journey. 💙🇬🇷
posts.cp: 9 years ago, we made a song called Santorini

Lord Voldemort’s name contains a hidden secret that reveals his true identity! In the Harry Potter series, “Tom Marvolo Riddle” is an anagram of “I am Lord Voldemort,” a clever detail created by author J.K. Rowling. Even more surprisingly, Voldemort was born on December 31, 1926, making him 71 years old when he died during the Battle of Hogwarts in 1998. Despite his obsession with immortality, he died younger than many ordinary wizards. Voldemort’s terrifying appearance wasn’t how he originally looked. As a young man, Tom Riddle was described as exceptionally handsome, but his experiments with dark magic gradually transformed his appearance. He created multiple Horcruxes by splitting his soul, believing they would protect him from death. Ironically, his desperate attempts to become immortal ultimately contributed to his destruction, making one of fiction’s most feared villains a character whose greatest weakness was his fear of dying. Unfortunately, this snake’s habitat is used frequently for agricultural purposes—growing coffee plants and ornamental ferns—which has decreased suitable habitat. You can do your part to protect the snake by purchasing wildlife-friendly coffee and growing plants native to your region in your outdoor spaces. posts.c: Glittering snow. The swoosh of skis; the scrape of skates. The hardcore coziness of Bernie mittens. We Vermonters cling to our wintry character as though to a toboggan flying down an icy hill. And yet as the climate warms, perhaps (with apologies to Noah Kahan) we should start to identify with a less flashy time of year: stick season. Wolcott artist Gabriel Tempesta (@gabrieltempesta) presents works portraying wild and rural scenes from throughout the year in “At the Edge of the Road … and Into the Woods,” on view through November 29 at Highland Center for the Arts in Greensboro. Even though the scent of apple blossoms is practically palpable in “Spring Queen,” and the artist pays careful attention to the hues of late-summer greenery in “Almost Full,” Tempesta’s paintings and drawings are rooted in this season’s decomposing leaves and heavy skies. He acknowledges as much in a statement introducing the show. In November, he writes, “Survival begins to seem more immediate.” Read the full

posts.c: Take a look at this melanistic leopard 🖤 "This photograph is one of my favorites of a very special creature, a female melanistic leopard named Giza, born in 2021 in the wilderness of Laikipia. If somebody had told me twenty years before that exactly on the day of my fiftieth birthday, August 19th 2025, I would be photographing a black leopard with a 50mm lens, I would have thought they were completely crazy! Until 2022, the mere possibility of even spotting a black leopard in Kenya was beyond anyone’s dream. But something incredible occurred in this rugged and wild region of Kenya. The melanistic gene began spreading successfully through the population of leopards, causing an increase in the incidence of this rare mutation. In a savannah habitat, black leopards would normally be disadvantaged, as they would be easy target for lions, and would be too visible to their prey. posts.c: Next Tuesday, November 24th, we're gathering downstairs for our monthly Helping Hands: Quilts for the Community event, and we would love for you to join us for the last sew-in of 2026. From 1 to 4pm, customers and staff come together to finish quilts that are donated to local organizations, including Laurie's House, Steps to End Domestic Violence, the Lund Home, the Respite House, and the Refugee Resettlement Center. It's one of our favorite afternoons of the month. Good people, good work, and a real sense of community. All skill levels are welcome, and there are plenty of jobs that don't require a sewing machine. We provide tables, chairs, cutting mats, irons, and ironing boards. posts.c: Spot the difference 👁️ Alex Visbal (@alexvisbal) is working on a long-term project documenting the industrial footprint on bodies of water, and this photo shows how a single engineered line can reshape an entire wetland. The distinctive pink colour on the left is caused by bright pink microbes that thrive in extremely saline water, which happens when an area is cut off from a supply of fresh water. The ecology of the lake is in sharp decline due to industrial use, upstream diversions and climate change. Since this image was taken, the State of Utah has brought the area under conservation management. 📸 ‘The Great Divide’ is the winner of the Wetlands: The Bigger Picture category in this year's Wildlife Photographer of the Year. Book your tickets for #WPY62 now via the link in our bio! #WPY #WildlifePhotographerOfTheYear #WildlifePhotography #NaturePhotography #NaturalHistoryMuseum #USA #Utah

posts.c: "紅葉 (kōyō) is the Japanese word for fall foliage," says CNT Local Creator @blindsaayintokyo. "It’s the moment when leaves start turning crimson red, bright yellow, and warm orange. Much like 桜 (sakura) in the spring, people across Japan (and plenty of visitors from abroad) make special trips out of the city for a chance at 紅葉狩り (momiji-gari), literally “maple-leaf hunting,” or the centuries-old practice of autumn foliage viewing. About two hours north of Tokyo in Tochigi Prefecture is 日光 (Nikkō), one of my favorite places for 紅葉狩り. Thanks to its wide range in elevation, Nikkō’s foliage peak cascades down the mountains over nearly two months. It starts at the wetlands of 戦場ヶ原 (Senjōgahara) in late September and ends in mid-November at the @unesco World Heritage shrine complex, home to 日光東照宮 (Nikkō Tōshō-gū). So no matter when you plan your trip to see the fall leaves, you’ll likely catch somewhere in Nikkō at peak color. Lucky! Add in the crisp, fresh mountain air, centuries-old cedar-l

posts.c: A caracal mother and cub 🧡 "When I moved to my tent just outside the Maasai Mara NR in 2007 and I became a full-time photographer, one particular creature was considered a sort of holy-grail for wildlife photographers working in Africa. It was rarely if ever seen, and the few sightings were just fleeting glimpses shooting across a track, or shadows in the dark night. One morning I was driving in the central Mara when I spotted a small predator jumping on a termite mound in the distance, immediately followed by a second one. I grabbed my binoculars and realised I was looking at two caracals. As they disappeared back in the long grass, I drove closer and after a long search, found them again, almost invisible, crouched in a small clump of grass. That moment marked the beginning of one of my most unforgettable stories in the wild. I followed this mother caracal and her curious male cub for a few months, until the evening when this photograph was taken, the last one they spent together bef

posts.c: “Touch grass” is an ancient internet expression used to remind people that there is an outside. An area beyond the computer or phone screen where plants grow and people occasionally make eye contact. Not too much eye contact. Let’s not be weird. The phrase is believed to have originated among online users who noticed that other online users were becoming increasingly unpleasant. Rather than explain this to them, they suggested they go outside and touch a plant. What did the plant ever do? Scientists have yet to establish whether touching grass actually improves someone’s mood or feelings. Early research suggests it does stop people from posting online anywhere between never and three seconds. It’s a start. The National Park Service has been encouraging people to get outdoors since 1916. So this weekend, consider logging off and getting outdoors. Your outlook on things might just improve. Have a great weekend. Tell us about it on Monday. NPS Photos

posts.c: Baseball fans have repeatedly told us they have two issues with the game today: blackouts and fairness We’re proposing to make three major changes to baseball: 1. Entering into a partnership with players where all revenues that are generated are split 50/50 between the teams and the players 2. Implementing a salary cap and floor that will regulate what each team can spend 3. Revenues from media generated in baseball are shared equally by the clubs This will reduce the revenue disparity in baseball and help us address local blackouts Major League players’ total compensation would go up and fans would get a more competitive game It’s a win for everybody

posts.c: The highly limited, large-scale collector’s edition of Reverence is officially available for purchase. Truthfully, when I asked for this edition to be made, I expected the answer to be “Impossible.” I am utterly obsessed with the idea of seeing my images printed as big as I can imagine. If I could see one of my icebergs or elephants the size of a building, looming larger than life, I would be over the moon. The challenge with printing images at such a scale is that quality tends to diminish as the pixels are stretched beyond their capacity. But the expert printers behind this very special edition of Reverence worked what can only be described as magic, bringing every detail into sharper focus than even my own memory. I call it the Jumbo Book: the definitive collection of my life’s work all compiled into one enormous volume of 160 print-sized images. posts.c: This is what we were up to while Outlook was down, if anyone was wondering. 🐟 Yesterday, @vtfishandwildlife fisheries biologists at the Ed Weed Fish Culture Station gave our team a demo on how they manage salmon traps in the fall! These salmon are captured during their fall migration up a small stream created by the hatchery's outflow. Biologists record data about the fish and take eggs from selected broodstock. Then, during the following spring and fall, young salmon raised at the hatchery are released into Lake Champlain and some inland waterways. This process is part of a broad effort to restore landlocked Atlantic salmon in Lake Champlain and support the lake's fishery. Photo 1: Sonya Vogel / LCBB; Photos 2-6: Emma Dannenberg/LCBP
posts.hd: Biologists demo salmon trap management at fish hatchery

posts.c: A bighorn sheep's face when someone says, "Nice antlers!" *bighorn sheep sigh* 😑 So, what's the difference between antlers and horns, anyway? Horns are a two-part structure. An interior portion of bone (which is an extension of the skull) is covered by an exterior sheath grown by specialized hair follicles (similar to human fingernails). Horns are usually found on both males and females of pronghorn, bison, and bighorn sheep. Antlers grow as an extension of the animal's skull. They are true bone, a single structure, and generally found only on males of the deer family. Antlers are also shed and re-grown each year, while horns are usually never shed and continue to grow throughout an animal's life. One exception to this rule is the pronghorn, which sheds and re-grows its horn sheath each year. Photo (NPS / Jacob W. Frank): 1. Bighorn sheep ram with large, curved horns. 2. Bull elk with large antlers. 3. Pronghorn buck with horns.
posts.cp: A bighorn sheep's face when someone says, "Nice antlers!"

Image description: A pair of overlapping spiral galaxies are seen merging into a single massive system. posts.c: Last week we finished up our first adult Learn to Ride class! This free multi week collaboration between Old Spokes Home and Local Motion offered instruction for folks learning to ride for the first time, and for others needing a refresher. This class contributes to Old Spokes Home's overall mission of removing barriers to make bikes work for everyone. It also aligns perfectly with Local Motion's mission of making it safe, accessible, and fun for everyone to bike, walk, and roll in Vermont. The ability to ride a bike, and to ride it safely, opens up opportunities at any age! This class eases students into riding by focusing on balance first. Bikes without cranks and pedals act as adult striders, and as students became more comfortable they work up to bikes with pedals. We'll be offering more FREE adult Learn to Ride classes in the spring!

posts.c: Saving a 136-year-old cast iron tub 🛁✨ Homeowners Harley and Ethan wanted to keep the original tub that came with the house, so @kevinoconnortoh and @dettmore101 took on the refinish together. Part 1: Stripping Suited up with respirators, since old paint can be lead-based Troweled on a ¼” layer of stripper paste Covered it with craft paper to keep it wet Let it work for 24 hours Bagged and sealed the paint, then scraped down to bare metal Part 2: Buffing + Painting Primed and sanded the outside Buffed the inside enamel with cerium oxide (a glass polish) and water Rinsed it, and the shine was back Flipped the tub and rolled on a matte black and white finish The matte finish hides the pitting and ties in with the tile Ready for another 130 years 🙌 📺 Watch today on @pbs (check local listings), and stream free Monday on @therokuchannel #TOHEssexCo #ThisOldHouse #TubRefinish #homeimprovement #beforeandafter

posts.c: 🍂Reconnect with your creative self this stick season and take a field trip to the BCA Center to experience Trystan Bates’ (@trystanbatesart) “Forms of Connection,” on view through January 23! ⁠ ⁠ Pop up to the second floor and dive into Bates’ exploration of storytelling, social interaction, and ritual as frameworks for understanding our shared experience. Through a process of collecting, abstracting, and rearranging information into symbolic visual forms, Bates distills ideas into geometric shapes and gestural elements. ⁠ ⁠ Moments of pause take center stage as space becomes an active element representing possibility, reflection, and unseen connections. These works are an evolution of Bates’ visual language, with isolated forms converging into dense, interlocking compositions, where every shape depends on the next. posts.c: Lava is hot. We thought you should know. We’ve been asked to elaborate. Fine. Lava is hot. It’s like making a grilled cheese, except the pan is a volcano on fire. Too much? Is it getting hot in here? Take two. Erupting lava at Hawaiʻi’s Kīlauea Volcano typically reaches around 2,100°F (1,150°C). That’s hot enough to turn rock into a glowing river of molten material. It’s also hot enough that getting too close can be extremely dangerous. Lava the view from a safe, designated viewing area, follow park guidance, and please resist the urge to find out just how hot it is firsthand. Some things are better left untouched. Lava is very high on that list. Has anyone touched lava lately? That’s not a question for you. We’re getting ahead of your questions. The answer, not that we know of. This is just a a friendly reminder to avoid any incidents. Plus even though lava is hot stuff, the pics are pretty cool to look at! NPS Photos: @hawaiivolcanoesnps /J. Wei
posts.hd: Lava fountain erupting at Kīlauea Volcano

The right hardware adds refinement, functionality, and a sense of weight that elevates the entire space. @rejuvenation has long been one of our favorite sources for timeless, high-quality pieces that feel both beautiful and intentional.⠀ ⠀ For our Maine kitchen, we leaned into unlacquered brass - a living finish that will naturally patina alongside the white oak cabinetry over time. posts.c: A cosmic sampler 🍽️ These images are all Hubble observations of gravitational lenses, a phenomenon that occurs when the gravity of a massive foreground object (such as a galaxy or cluster of galaxies) bends, warps, and magnifies the light from a more distant background object. Hubble's targets show the diversity of how this effect can appear. Plus, these observations lay the groundwork for follow-up observations by the new Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope. While Hubble gets a better view of individual lenses, Roman will be able to capture many more lenses with its wider field-of-view. If Roman finds a particularly interesting lens, researchers may use Hubble to take follow-up observations using its visible and ultraviolet prowess for individual objects. Learn more at the link in our bio! Image credit: NASA, ESA, and X. Huang (University of San Francisco); Processing: Gladys Kober (NASA/Catholic University of America) Image description: A nine-image panel, each showing a different grav

posts.c: Rifle season opens this Saturday, and before everyone heads out into the woods, we wanted to help everyone have a safe and successful hunt by addressing a few Frequently Asked Questions we’ve been receiving: Q: Can I still hunt archery during rifle season? A: Rifle season & archery season are two completely separate seasons, each with their own regulations, with dates that overlap. Follow the regulations based on type of hunting you want to do, and which tags you have. For example, if a hunter wants to take a deer using their rifle tag, then they will hunt under rifle season regulations. If they’d like to take a deer using their archery tag, then they would hunt with their bow and under archery season regulations. Q: If a hunter is archery hunting, can they take an antlerless deer anywhere in the state? A: Yes, the archery season allows you to take an antlerless deer statewide. The hunter would tag with their archery tag and follow all archery regulations. Q: If a hunter has an antlerl

posts.c: Burying food scraps in your garden sounds like an easy way to feed your plants, but there’s a little more soil science involved than you might think. Organic matter doesn’t become plant food overnight. Soil microbes, fungi, and other decomposers have to break it down first, converting complex organic compounds into simpler nutrients that plant roots can eventually absorb. Here’s the catch: decomposition takes time, and fresh organic materials can temporarily tie up nutrients as microbes consume them to do their work. Depending on the material, its carbon-to-nitrogen ratio, and how quickly it breaks down, burying food scraps can actually delay nutrient availability rather than give plants an immediate boost. Materials like raw animal tissue also need time to decompose, which can make nutrient release unpredictable. The real lesson is that feeding your soil isn’t just about what you bury, but how quickly that material becomes available to your plants. Finished compost has already gone th

posts.c: We’re travelling with Doodle again, and again with @akasaair 🐶✈️ After our last flight, I got so many DMs asking how I prepare Doodle, crate train him, which crate we use and what I pack, so here’s everything I do before we fly. Honestly, most of the preparation happens before you even reach the airport. 🐾 Crate prep: I keep Doodle’s crate around for a few days before the flight so he can get comfortable going in, chilling and sleeping in it. 📦 Right-size crate: Doodle’s crate is 32 inches. Make sure your pet can comfortably stand, turn around and lie down. I also use a crate with removable wheels for easier handling. 🧸 Familiar comforts: His familiar comforter and favourite toy always go inside, something that smells like home helps him feel more settled. For anxious pets: If your pet gets anxious, speak to your vet about vet-approved calming support, which may be started a few days to a week before travel. posts.c: When Yellowstone was established in 1872, the National Park Service did not yet exist (and wouldn't until 1916). The park's first civilian superintendents lacked experience, funds, and a workforce to protect the park from exploitation. Eventually, Company M, First U.S. Cavalry of Ft. Custer, Montana Territory, answered the call to come to Yellowstone in 1886. This started the 30+ years of military protection of Yellowstone National Park. From the beginnings of Yellowstone to modern day, and all the time in between, we thank those who have served in the U.S. Armed Forces and continue to serve in a different uniform for the NPS. #VeteransDay 👉 Take a walking tour of the Fort Yellowstone Historic District or check out our virtual tour to learn more: https://www.nps.gov/thingstodo/yell-tour-fort-yellowstone.htm (available in our bio) Photos (from the NPS Historical Archive and Jacob W. Frank): 1. Mounted cavalry drill on Fort Yellowstone's Parade Ground in Mammoth Hot Springs (c. 1910) 2.

posts.c: @rc.s is no stranger to the world stage. We caught up with him before the season kicked off to ask him a few questions... With the Olympics under your belt, what are you taking along with you this winter, and what are you leaving behind? “I’m taking the confidence of knowing that my best skiing is strong enough to compete with the rest of the best in the world. I’ve had plenty of successful races, including at the Olympics, and I’m proud of the results I’ve worked hard for. I can also look back and see that my mindset at the Olympics was no different from many of the less significant days. The most important thing has been finding presence in the moment and embracing the challenge head on and with a positive attitude. I’m leaving behind the weight that gets put on any one race. Every season has its ups and downs, and no single result defines it.” Read the full Q&A at the 🔗 in bio.

Many arguments have arose about what Government mean[t] to do with above prisoners; the great number of our men in the hands of the Provincials, will surely prevent our proceeding with severity towards them. posts.c: Powering up research!☀️⚡ Last week, space station astronauts installed the eighth and final roll-out solar array (ROSA), completing a five-year power upgrade. Roll-out solar arrays have a lightweight and compact design that launches as a cylinder and unfurls like a yoga mat after installation. Despite being about half the size of the legacy arrays, the eight additional roll-out solar arrays boost the station’s power generation by more than 160 kilowatts. Together, the arrays provide increased power for daily operations and hundreds of research investigations that benefit humanity and support future exploration missions. Following prior testing on space station, the roll-out solar arrays have also been used on NASA’s Dart mission, showcasing space station’s essential role as a testbed for the technologies needed for expeditions beyond Earth’s orbit.
posts.hd: Final roll-out solar array installed on space station

🍟 80 YEARS OF FRENCH FRY HISTORY! Since 1946, Al’s French Frys in South Burlington, Vermont, has been serving up crispy golden fries and classic roadside favorites. What started as a small roadside fry stand founded by Al and Genevieve Rusterholz grew into one of Vermont’s most beloved food institutions. In 2010, Al’s earned the prestigious James Beard Foundation America’s Classics Award, recognizing its place in American food culture. Nearly eight decades later, the tradition lives on with the same old-school charm that made this place special in the first place. posts.c: Calling all teachers, educators and homeschoolers: now is the time to sign up for Scat & Tracks! This fun, educational program is designed to get students from kindergarten through eighth grade outside and exploring Vermont's landscapes and local wildlife by giving educators the plans and support they need to lead nature hikes on school or nearby grounds. Each week for four weeks, students will watch a pre-recorded video that focuses on one Vermont species and covers topics such as habitat, lifecycle and natural history facts. After the video, the students head outside with their teacher to look for the appropriate habitat of the animal that was featured, paying close attention to scat, tracks, and other signs of the critter. This year's featured species includes moose, long-tailed weasel, eastern cottontail, and red fox! The deadline to register is December 15th. Don't wait! Sign up today at https://www.vtfishandwildlife.com/learn-more/conservation-education/scat-and-tracks-program

posts.c: Asparagus is a perennial because it has an underground storage system that keeps it coming back year after year. The crown, a cluster of buds and roots just below the soil, stores carbohydrates that fuel new spear growth every spring. Its deep, established root system also helps the plant access water and nutrients beyond the reach of many shallow-rooted vegetables. Here’s the interesting part: those feathery ferns aren’t just extra foliage. They’re the plant’s solar panels. Through photosynthesis, they capture sunlight and convert it into sugars, which are transported down to the crown and stored as energy reserves. The more energy the crown accumulates during the growing season, the more resources it has to produce healthy spears in the seasons ahead. That’s why harvesting asparagus too early can set the plant back. Every spear you cut is a potential fern that could have been producing energy for the underground crown. Letting those spears mature allows the plant to build the reserve

posts.c: Across the National Park System, forts, battlefields, historic homes and coastal defenses preserve the places where military history unfolded, and the stories of the people who lived it. At Minute Man National Historical Park, follow the route where the opening battles of the American Revolution began. At Gettysburg National Military Park, walk through the landscape that witnessed one of the Civil War’s defining battles. At Fort McHenry National Monument & Historic Shrine, discover the story behind the flag that inspired “The Star-Spangled Banner.” And at Pearl Harbor National Memorial, remember the lives forever changed by the events of December 7, 1941. From Revolutionary War battlefields to World War II installations and Cold War defenses, these places connect us to generations of service, sacrifice and the lasting impact of conflict. posts.c: Earth’s protective ozone layer is still on track for long-term recovery, despite a larger Antarctic ozone hole this year. The 2026 ozone hole is the 7th-largest ozone hole since NASA began tracking it in 1979. This year, the ozone hole reached its maximum extent of 10.5 million square miles on September 18. However, the ozone hole could have been 1 to 2 million square miles larger if ozone-depleting substances were as prevalent in the atmosphere today as they were two decades ago. posts.c: 🎾 Seasonal tennis courts shut down — starting the week of November 9, @btvparks will begin removing tennis and pickleball nets from courts throughout Burlington and turning off the overhead lights at the Leddy Park courts. At all court facilities, except for Schmanska Park, one court will remain available through the end of November. Removing the nets helps protect court surfaces and infrastructure during the winter months. Freeze-thaw cycles, combined with the tension on the nets, place additional stress on pavement and net anchors, increasing the risk of cracks and damage to both pavement and concrete. Thanks for your partnership!

posts.c: One of the things I find most extraordinary about polar bears is the immense journeys they undertake over a lifetime. Guided by a sense of smell seven times more powerful than a blood hound’s, they can detect a seal hidden beneath layers of snow and ice from more than half a mile away. They spend much of their lives following invisible trails of scent across hundreds of miles of Arctic wilderness. This is also how they find one another across a vast, seemingly desolate landscape, although finding mates has become more of a challenge as sea ice recedes. They are the great nomads of the Arctic, always inquisitive, resourceful, and, above all, fiercely determined to navigate a formidable and ever-changing world. For those interested in owning one of my polar bear prints, please visit the link in my bio or visit my website to submit an inquiry. From now until Christmas, all fine art purchases come with a copy of my new book Reverence.

Our founder spoke at a recent Burlington City Council meeting to advocate for change to the Burlington Forward resolution. "I have deep concerns that this resolution, both in its original form and as it currently exists, deepens the stigma and judgment our neighbors face daily." "..when I was homeless, this was one of my biggest fears. That people would judge me for existing while homeless. My fears were founded, and if you are homeless, your life is on display for the public’s enjoyment and abuse. Can you imagine what that feels like? I will never forget it." #NothingAboutUsWithoutUs #Burlington #Vermont #LetsWorkTogether #EndTheStigma

posts.c: It's #NationalBisonDay, and we've got some bison facts! 1️⃣ Bison are the largest land mammal in North America Male bison (bulls) weigh up to 2,000 pounds and stand 6 feet tall, while females (cows) weigh up to 1,000 pounds and reach a height of 4-5 feet. Bison calves can weigh 30–70 pounds at birth. 2️⃣ Bison may be big, but they're also fast They are extremely agile and can run up to 30 miles per hour! 3️⃣ You can judge a bison's mood by its tail When it hangs down and swishes naturally, the bison is usually calm. If the tail is standing straight up, watch out! It may be ready to charge. No matter what a bison's tail is doing though, remember that they are unpredictable and can charge at any moment. Every year, there are regrettable accidents caused by people getting too close to these massive animals. It's great to love the bison but always be sure to love them from a distance of at least 25 yards (23 meters). 4️⃣ Bison love a good salad They primarily eat grasses, weeds and leafy p

posts.c: Hubble (along with ground-based telescopes) revealed that the expansion rate of our universe is accelerating! Soon, the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope will study the “dark energy” behind this expansion with its large field of view and infrared vision. Its treasure trove of data will include tens of thousands of exploding stars and hundreds of millions of distant galaxies, tracing the universe’s expansion across nearly all of cosmic history! Hubble's key observations led to dark energy's discovery (even helping earn a Nobel prize in physics!) and the mission will work with Roman to continue investigating this enigma. As we gear up for its first images, we'll share more here on how Roman and Hubble bring different superpowers to astronomy. posts.c: Warm fall days mean more time on the trails, and at Catamount Outdoor Family Center, we love to see it! 🍂 Before you head home, make a quick tick check for you and your family a routine. Ticks stay active in the fall, especially on milder days, and they can be tiny. Here are some tips to help protect yourself this fall: 🧦 Dress for it: wear light-colored long pants and long sleeves, and tuck your pants into your socks before heading out. 🔍 Check the hard-to-see places: your scalp, behind your ears, your armpits, behind your knees, and your waistband. 👕 Toss your clothes in the dryer for 10 minutes on high heat when you get home. 🚿 Shower as soon as you’re done outside for the day. 🐾 Don’t forget to check your kids, gear, and pets too! Learn more at HealthVermont.gov/BeTickSmart. Come prepared and head home tick-free. Happy trails! 👣 #CatamountCommunity #TickAware #GetOutside #OutdoorRecreation #Vermont #Hike #Bike #Run #Walk

You've likely heard of geysers and hot springs, but what about fumaroles? Fumaroles (or steam vents) are the hottest hydrothermal features in Yellowstone, with temperatures up to 280 F (138 C)! 🔥 Because they are so hot and contain very little water, the water boils away before reaching the surface. Then, steam and other gases emerge from the feature's vent, sometimes making hissing or whistling sounds. Roaring Mountain is a wonderful place to enjoy the sights and sounds of fumaroles, especially on cooler days! 👉 Learn more about fumaroles at: go.nps.gov/YELLhydrothermalfeatures (link in our "Learn More" highlight) Photo (NPS / Ashton Hooker): Roaring Mountain on a chilly winter day.

posts.c: Each autumn, we return to Twilight of the Idols, our seasonal porter brewed with coffee and cinnamon and conditioned on vanilla beans. Its origins precede Hill Farmstead, reaching back to Denmark in 2009. Shaun and Ryan Witter-Merithew first met in 2007. Two years later, as Shaun prepared to leave his brewing position at Nørrebro Bryghus and Fanø Bryghus, he enticed Ryan to move to Denmark to assume the role. They lived and brewed together for a month, beginning a friendship and collaboration that continues today. During that overlap, they established Grassroots Brewing to continue making beer together and maintain their connection to Denmark. Working on their first Christmas beer together (Fanø’s JulePorter), the idea for what would become Twilight of the Idols emerged from this period, taking its name from Friedrich Nietzsche’s text. Birth of Tragedy, Six Years, Phenomenology of Spirit, and Viola Sofia also became part of their shared work. Here in Greensboro, the porter has become a

posts.c: What if your fence could grow food instead of just taking up space? A fruit fence turns a simple vertical structure into a productive growing system, and passion fruit is perfect for the job because its climbing tendrils naturally grip onto nearby supports. The science is pretty cool. Passion fruit vines grow rapidly, spreading their leaves across a trellis to capture sunlight for photosynthesis. With enough light, water, and nutrients, the plant converts that energy into vigorous growth and eventually flowers and fruit. Training the vines vertically also helps you use space more efficiently, turning an otherwise unused area into productive growing space. And here’s the best part: a well-established passion fruit vine can produce an impressive harvest while giving you a living privacy screen. Instead of building a fence that only blocks the view, why not grow one that hides the eyesores, adds greenery, and produces delicious fruit? That’s a whole lot more value from the same footprint.
posts.hd: Passion fruit vines grown as a fruit fence

posts.c: Small plants need love too! So I try to find a fun way to style them instead of just placing them in a standard terra cotta pot. Here, I took this 4” birkin philodendron and cut the perfect piece of cork to surround its roots. Instead of glue a stainless steel mesh base to the cork, like I typically do, I used a low planter to work as the base of the “pot” to hold in the soil. Obviously it has drainage holes for those that were about to ask 😉 I then dressed up the topsoil with live moss and called it a day. It might be small but it makes a strong statement 💚🌿 #plants #plantstyling #design #beforeandafter #babygirl Low planter from @fayraystudio

posts.c: Have you ever wondered how birds stay warm during winter? Chickadees grow feathers that can keep them up to 100 degrees F warmer than the surrounding air temperature. Waterfowl exhibit counter-current heat exchange in their limbs, which enables them to stand in cold water. Other adaptations include roosting with heads tucked into back feathers to conserve heat and staying active by retrieving food stored during the autumn months. 👉 Want to learn more? Visit the link in our “Learn More” highlight! Photos (NPS / Jim Peaco & Jacob W. Frank): (1) Mountain chickadee (2) Mallards on Alum Creek

posts.c: We don’t need another reason to love creativity, but research linking arts participation to slower biological aging is a pretty good one. 🎨 A recent University College London study found that more frequent engagement in arts and cultural activities was associated with slower biological aging. Weekly arts participants showed a 4% slower pace of aging than those who rarely participated. Here’s why this matters for play. Art is one way we play. When we paint, dance, make music, experiment with materials, or create something alongside others, we’re engaging in the very things that make play powerful: curiosity, imagination, expression, and exploration. The research gives us another reason to take these experiences seriously. Play isn’t just entertainment or a break from real life. It’s part of how we nurture our creativity, connection, and vitality. Make something. Move something. Try something new. Give yourself the gift ofplay. #PlayIntention #PowerOfPlay #CreativeWellbeing #ArtsAndHealt

posts.c: I wish they had the slightest idea that how much they mean to us. Just yesterday, one of our cats disappeared out of sight for a few minutes as I’d left her chilling in the backyard. These are indoor cats, so they have absolutely zero clue about life beyond the four walls of our home & the little garden they know so well. And in those few moments, I went through an entire range of emotions. From panic to worry, from imagining all sorts of terrible possibilities to the fear of not knowing where she had gone. Meanwhile, 🐈 walked back in, completely unbothered, after her antics. 🤦🏻‍♀️ Also, as a cat owner, if there’s one thing I could recommend, it would be investing in a self-cleaning litter box. It has genuinely changed our lives, especially in a multi-cat household. Ours is a pretty old model, so it’s too big compared to the much smarter ones available these days. 🤌🏼 - - - #livingroom #bedroom #bluebedroom #cosybedroom #bedroomideas

posts.c: The stars are just the night sky's mice... The first image is Webb's near-infrared view of the Cat's Head Nebula, a star-forming region. Webb can see through the opaque clouds of dust and gas to see the stars forming within. One of these makes up the cat's glowing "eye" and another, with Webb's characteristic eight-pointed diffraction spikes, its whiskers. The second slide shows Webb's mid-infrared look at the Cat's head, the dust shining brightly. There are structures to the left of the cat visible in the infrared that do not appear in @NASAHubble's visible light view (third slide). The cat's eye is reddish here, glowing from inside the dust. The bright yellow ridge along the cat's "chest" shows gas illuminated and ionized by ultraviolet radiation from nearby massive stars. Happy Halloween! Credits: Image: NASA, ESA, STScI; Image Processing: Joseph DePasquale (STScI) Read more at the link in our bio. Image description in comments.

posts.c: New Tools for Healthier Soils! We’ve got new equipment at the Intervale Center! Thanks to funding from the Vermont Housing and Conservation Board and the Vermont Agency of Agriculture, our new 6-foot seed drill and flail mower will make it easier to plant and manage crops across the Intervale. Right now, we are planting cover crops. Cover crops are planted to protect the soil between growing seasons, rather than for harvest. Their roots hold soil in place, build organic matter, and reduce nutrient runoff; creating a strong, resilient foundation for our food system. The seed drill plants seeds with minimal soil disturbance, and the mower chops down vegetation for quick and efficient turnover back to crop production. Their compact size makes them ideal for smaller farm fields and garden plots in the Intervale that were formerly cover cropped by hand or not at all. These tools will support Intervale Center land stewardship, Intervale farmers, the Intervale Conservation Nursery, and agrofo

posts.c: Comment ‘dad’ on this post for an extra dad joke straight to your DM’s 👇 Cars use several types of filters to protect their engines, improve performance, and keep passengers comfortable. Air filters prevent dust and dirt from entering the engine, oil filters remove contaminants from engine oil, and fuel filters stop impurities from reaching the fuel system. These filters help reduce wear, improve efficiency, and extend the lifespan of important components. Cabin air filters also clean the air entering the passenger compartment, trapping dust, pollen, and other airborne particles. Interestingly, a clogged filter can reduce engine performance, restrict airflow, or cause unpleasant smells inside the car, depending on which filter is affected. Regular filter replacement is one of the simplest ways to keep a vehicle running smoothly.

posts.c: If you ask us, the longline tuna fishery in Hawaii is making waves! 🐟🌺 Solid fishery management can make even the less-selective fishing methods more ocean-friendly. Hawaii is leading the charge by making its longline fishery more environmentally sustainable. This means: ✅ switching from less than 20% human observer coverage to 100% electronic camera monitoring by 2027 to track bycatch and gather data for fishery management decisions. ✅ training fishers to safely handle and release accidentally caught species like sharks, turtles, seabirds, and marine mammals. ✅ gear modifications to reduce seabird interactions. ✅ strategic area closures to protect vulnerable species. and more! The future for longline tuna fishing in Hawaii is bright.☀️ Look for yellow- and green-rated tuna caught in Hawaii for your next sustainable meal. What is making this sea of sand march inland? ⌛ This timelapse shows the Lençóis Maranhenses National Park in northeastern Brazil, known for its large sand dunes and seasonal rainwater lagoons. Strong winds from the Atlantic Ocean keep these dunes in constant motion. Over the years, the wind steadily pushes the sand, causing the dunes to migrate inland and change the shape of the landscape. Satellite data helps scientists track how remote landscapes change over time. Captured by the joint @nasa and @usgs Landsat program, these natural-color images show over four decades of this moving environment. Video description: A natural-color Landsat time series of Brazil’s Lençóis Maranhenses National Park spanning from 1984 to 2026. As the video plays, large white sand dunes move steadily inland across the coast. Among the shifting white sand are darker patches of seasonal rainwater lagoons and vegetation. #nasa #earth #science

posts.c: We’re not kitten around! @NASAHubble and @NASAWebb captured a purr-fect view of the Cat’s Head Nebula. This long thin structure, made of dark, dense dust, looks like the head of a cat, its eye a newborn star still shrouded by the dust and gas from which it formed. Hubble and Webb’s contrasting and complementary views give us a fuller picture of the features of this object. In the mid-infrared, as seen by Webb, the dust shines brightly while in the near-infrared, Webb can see through the dust to the stars hidden within. In visible light, Hubble's view shows a dark brown pillar of dust, with a yellow ridge along the right side. This bright rim shows gas illuminated and ionized by ultraviolet radiation from nearby massive stars. On the left are some dust pillars seen in the mid-infrared that are not observed in visible light. It's paw-sible to "fly through" these views with the help of visualizations created by (human) data scientists, which bring Hubble and Webb observations to un-fur-ge

While El Niño occurs in the Pacific Ocean, with changes most visible along the equator, its effects can be felt all around the world. NASA satellites like PACE and Sentinel-6 are equipped to measure some of the key features of the phenomenon. posts.c: Hardneck garlic relies on a process called vernalization, where prolonged exposure to cold temperatures triggers the physiological changes needed for proper bulb development. Without enough chilling, the plant may grow leaves but struggle to form the full, well-developed bulbs you want. Refrigerating hardneck garlic for about two months can help simulate winter, even in a warm climate. That cold exposure influences the plant’s growth signals, helping prepare it for the transition into active growth once temperatures rise. It’s essentially giving the garlic the seasonal cue it needs, without having to live somewhere with an actual winter. Once you plant those chilled cloves, they can resume growth with the cold requirement better satisfied, improving the chances of developing well-formed bulbs. It’s a great example of how understanding a plant’s biology lets you work around your climate instead of being limited by it.

posts.c: Hanging peppers might look like an old-school gardening trick, but there’s some cool science behind it. When you hang peppers to dry, moisture gradually evaporates from their skin and inner tissues into the surrounding air. The key is airflow and low humidity, which help carry that moisture away so the peppers can dry more efficiently. As their water content drops, it becomes harder for many spoilage microbes to grow, helping preserve your harvest for longer. Here’s why the way you string them matters, too. Threading through the calyx, the leafy cap at the top of the pepper, helps avoid puncturing the fleshy fruit, where damaged tissue and trapped moisture can encourage rot. Give your peppers a dry, well-ventilated spot, and you’re using evaporation and moisture control to turn a fresh harvest into a longer-lasting supply of homegrown heat.

posts.c: This planet is haunted! 👻 The ghosts of volcanic eruptions, asteroid strikes, and evaporated lakes here on Earth are visible in echoes seen from space. Explore some of the places on our planet still haunted by the past. A volcanic eruption about 4,000 years ago created the eerily named Deception Island. The horseshoe-shaped island is actually the exposed part of a volcano itself, while the harbor in its center is a phantom of that massive volcanic eruption. As the volcano’s magma chamber emptied, the sudden drop in pressure inside the volcano caused the top to collapse and form a caldera — now called Port Foster. Image description: Landsat 8 image of Deception Island. It is horseshoe shaped and mostly rocky brown. The thin arch of rock comes to a ridge that runs the length of the island, along its center, like a backbone. posts.c: We asked this 8-year-old to draw the famous “Cosmic Cliffs” hidden within the Carina Nebula, based on the famous James Webb Space Telescope image. The region is actually the edge of a gigantic, gaseous cavity within NGC 3324, roughly 7,600 light-years away. The cavernous area has been carved from the nebula by the intense ultraviolet radiation and stellar winds from extremely massive, hot, young stars located in the center of the bubble, above the area shown in this image. The high-energy radiation from these stars is sculpting the nebula’s wall by slowly eroding it away. Our artist managed to capture the beauty of this Webb image, along with her version of the telescope itself, a rocket ship, and there is even a cameo of "The Traveler" exploring the cosmos! Optical illusions happen because your eyes send information to your brain, and your brain immediately starts making educated guesses about what it is seeing. Usually that works perfectly, but certain patterns, colors, shadows, and shapes can trick those shortcuts, making still images appear to move or identical lines look completely different. The best part is that even after someone explains the illusion, your brain may still refuse to cooperate. You can literally know two squares are the same color and your brain will look you dead in the eye and say, “No, they absolutely are not.” Like this content? Follow us for more @dadsaysjokes ❤️

held.c: Thom Lauzon, the longtime mayor of Barre whose dual roles as its most vocal booster and largest property developer left an indelible mark on the city and at times courted controversy, has died unexpectedly. He was 65. Lauzon was six months into his eighth term as mayor, after winning a close election in May. The Barre-Montpelier Time-Argus first reported the mayor’s death, the cause of which Vermont Public has not yet confirmed. In a statement, Gov. Phil Scott, a Barre native who counted Lauzon as an ally, said Lauzon’s death is a “gigantic loss” for the Granite City. “Like many, I’m shocked and saddened,” Scott said. “Thom was always ready, willing and able to help someone in need and take on a challenge. That can-do attitude was evident to everyone he crossed paths with. He was truly the spark behind so much of the progress Barre has made over the years.” Read the full story at the link in our bio. Photo by Zoe McDonald/Vermont Public.
held.hd: Barre Mayor Thom Lauzon dies at 65

As we continue to grieve Nipho alongside you, we’re sharing what we’ve learned about his passing, along with an update on his half-brother, Sundzu. Inhlonipho “Nipho," passed away on Wednesday after a brief battle with one of the most serious diseases facing the world’s elephants, known as EEHV-HD (elephant endotheliotropic herpesvirus hemorrhagic disease). EEHV-HD, which poses no risk to people or other wildlife, is caused by a naturally occurring virus found in Asian and African elephants around the world, both in their native habitats and human care. Most elephants will contract the virus in their lifetime, and many carry it without becoming ill. Younger elephants are particularly vulnerable to complications. Nipho’s illness came on and progressed unusually fast. Our team began treatment right away, even before a definitive diagnosis, and we are continuing to look closely at his case to understand what happened. It is with exceptionally heavy hearts that we share the passing of Inhlonipho “Nipho,” an incomparable African savanna elephant at the San Diego Zoo. As with all wildlife at the Zoo, Nipho’s wellness was monitored closely each day. When his team noticed signs of stomach discomfort and lethargy, the Zoo’s wildlife health experts provided prompt, around-the-clock care. Despite their tireless efforts, Nipho passed away today with his wildlife care specialists by his side. Nipho was deeply rooted in the San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance family. He was born at the San Diego Zoo Safari Park to his mom, Umngani, who continues to thrive in the Elephant Valley herd. Throughout his life at both the Safari Park and the Zoo, he opened the door for countless guests to connect with his endangered species, a fitting legacy for an elephant whose name means “courteous.” As he grew older, Nipho followed the path of young males in native habitats, who leave their family herds and may form bachelor herds to

held.c: Last week was tough for us. We were about to go on our daily walk, Kiki was on the couch while I put her harness on, I quickly went upstairs, and when I came back down, she was laying on the floor acting strange. When she got up, she was panting, drooling, and lifting her paw. It was 4pm on a Sunday, which meant the vets were closed. We had to drive 25 minutes to an emergency vet, they gave her pain meds and told us to keep an eye on her. On Monday morning, she was visibly in pain - as you can see in the first few clips. So we took her to the vet again. They told us - she has no noticeable fractures so you can either wait it out with her pain meds, or do an xray to find out more. We wanted to know more. And thank goodness we did… as it turned out, Kiki had hip dysplasia. One that you can tell it has most likely been there since she was a puppy - some dogs get it genetically. Ok people, It is Election Day and I hope you all know what that means! Time to go VOTE!! If you are like me, you may be saddened by the current political state in our country. Party allegiance aside, so much of what is being talked about seems to be fueled by hatred, violence and struggle. While It can all feel overwhelming, I always try and remember that the actual people who live in this country are loving, kind, hard working and resilient. When I was greeted with the above spread I was reminded about how great the people are and how important It is to elect leaders who think and act like us. The vast majority of us still do things because It helps to lift up our people, not because It is going to make us a billion dollars. This Election Day I will vote for the hard working Americans who deserve a better and easier path forward, and I will vote against the greedy and power obsessed billionaires who think they can run this country. It’s Pop-up week 🔍 What exactly is “slow looking”? Slow looking is an approach to viewing art that emphasizes our own observations and reflections, rather than familiarity with the artwork or art terminology. It’s also a visual thinking strategy used by first-year medical students in Dr. Sakshi Jasra’s Professionalism, Communication, and Reflection class at the Larner College of Medicine. Now in it’s third year running with the Fleming, we partnered with Dr. Jasra to transform her popular assignment into a pop-up exhibit for all! Now through Saturday, visit the Learning Studio to visit “Double Take” any time during our regular hours and try slow looking for yourself. Featuring a wide range of works from our collections, including a clay tablet from Mesopotamia, a photograph by Carrie Mae Weems, and much more, simply choose a work and follow our prompts. The only thing you need to bring is your own curiosity.
